question: Trace how our understanding of water on Mars changed over time.

sub_questions: What did early telescopic and Viking-era observations imply about surface water on Mars?
What orbital imaging and spectroscopy revealed about ancient flowing water (valley networks, outflow channels, hydrated minerals)?
What in‑situ rover and lander discoveries (rounded pebbles, conglomerates, clays, sulfates) changed interpretations of past aqueous environments?
What evidence has been found for present-day water or ice (polar caps, ground ice, transient surface flows) and how did that view evolve?
phrasings: Trace how our understanding of water on Mars changed over time.
Early telescopic observations showed bright polar caps and seasonal changes on Mars.
Viking landers examined soil chemistry and searched for signs of water-related processes.
Orbital images revealed extensive valley networks and outflow channels consistent with ancient flowing water.
High-resolution orbital spectroscopy detected clay minerals and sulfates formed in aqueous environments.
The first of two rovers landed and began sending back close-up views of rocks and pebbles.
The twin rovers explored ancient streambeds and found rounded pebbles and sedimentary textures indicating sustained flow.
Curiosity analyzed fluvial conglomerates and detected mineral assemblages consistent with long-lived freshwater lakes.
visual_phrasings: Wide-angle orbital mosaic showing valley networks, outflow channels and layered basin deposits on Mars.
Rover close-ups of rounded pebbles, cross-bedded sedimentary layers and conglomerate rocks with wheel tracks nearby.
Orbital spectral maps overlaid on surface images highlighting clay- and sulfate-rich regions, and images of polar layered ice caps.
Slope-facing dark streaks on crater walls (recurring slope lineae) and exposed subsurface ice in high-latitude trenches.
plan.rationale: I split the broad question into four chronological strands—early telescopic/Viking hints, orbital geomorphology and mineralogy, rover/lander in‑situ sedimentary and chemical evidence, and modern evidence for present ice/transient water—to map narration and visuals in NASA archive language for retrieval.

answer.answer: Early mission retrospectives note that what we once did not know about Mars later included the existence of very large subsurface glaciers and substantial frozen water reservoirs [2].  In the 2000s, rover and orbiter work shifted the picture from vague possibility to specific chemical and geomorphic clues: rovers found salts whose depth correlates with how much water once flowed, and orbiters mapped terraced, scalloped impact features consistent with past water-related processes [6][8].  By the 2010s scientists framed open questions about how much water Mars had and how it was lost, while also proposing persistent surface waters billions of years ago that could have shaped the landscape [11][12].  Most recently, Perseverance and Curiosity are examining ancient river channels and layered bedrock that tie the chemical and orbital hints to direct sedimentary evidence of past flowing water in particular places [13][14].

chronology.claim: Retrospective accounts of the Mariner era emphasize that Mars hosts large subsurface glaciers and significant frozen water, a conclusion drawn in later summaries of early missions [2].

Rover observations in the 2000s found salt deposits whose depth implies more extensive past water flow, while orbiters revealed crater and terrain features consistent with water-related modification [6][8].

By the mid-2010s researchers were explicitly asking how much water Mars once had and how it was lost, and considered that persistent surface waters billions of years ago could have fashioned much of the terrain [11][12].

In the 2020s rover missions are directly studying ancient river channels and layered sedimentary rocks, linking earlier chemical and orbital evidence to localized sedimentary records of flowing water [13][14].

answer.caveats: Many of the eras attached to these clips come from the archive labels (video or published) rather than independent dating of the original events (see examples [2], [6], [14]). The clips summarize and connect different lines of evidence but do not by themselves quantify total water volumes or precisely date when water was present or lost on Mars [11].

evidence.text: Grainy, desaturated footage of a small four‑wheeled lunar vehicle traveling across a rocky, powdery regolith. The camera view is from behind and slightly above the vehicle looking forward over its rear rack and wheel assemblies; a looped white cable or tether lies on the surface to the left of the rover. The plain is scattered with small angular rocks and pebbles and shows distinct wheel/track marks. In the midground a low, rounded hill or dome rises against a stark black sky (no atmosphere visible). Equipment boxes, structural frame elements and a boxy component on the rover’s rear are visible but no identifying markings or readable on‑screen readouts appear. The spoken narration (provided separately) refers to driving 16 miles on the lunar surface.

evidence.query: Wide-angle orbital mosaic showing valley networks, outflow channels and layered basin deposits on Mars.
evidence.text: A montage of Mars maps and orbital images arranged on a black background. Left: a large, colorized orbital view of a dune-filled crater with the bold label "Belva" over it. A white line with small circular waypoints and a blue rover-pin icon traces a rover route along the left margin of that crater. Right: a 2x3 grid of close-up crater images (likely HiRISE/CTX) showing different morphologies — a scalloped rim crater with sunlit edges, a dune-filled bowl, a crater with bright bluish/radial ejecta, and a high-relief rim crater rendered in grayscale. Another panel shows a regional colored topographic map with a red pin and the label "JEZERO CRATER," plus a contour/topography inset credited to the EUROPEAN SPACE AGENCY; a USGS polar/global Mars map is also visible in an upper frame. Imagery includes colorized elevation shading, false-color enhanced ejecta, and high-resolution surface photography; no instrument readouts or mission clocks are visible in the frames.
evidence.title: How Does NASA Name Things on Mars? (Mars Report - June 2023)

evidence.query: Rover close-ups of rounded pebbles, cross-bedded sedimentary layers and conglomerate rocks with wheel tracks nearby.
evidence.text: Close-up color views from a rover on a dusty, rocky plain. Foreground: the rover’s instrument turret at the end of the robotic arm is centered over a rounded, flat-topped rock; the turret shows multiple cylindrical and box-shaped sensor/actuator housings and a visible shadow cast onto the regolith. A rover wheel and part of the suspension are visible at left. Surrounding terrain is a mix of small pebbles, wind-blown sand, and larger fractured slabs; low ridges or cratered hills appear on the horizon. Also included are several close-up color frames of rock surface texture showing layered, fractured, and pitted material with loose orange-brown dust in depressions and darker, harder-looking patches. One grayscale wide-angle image shows a smooth sandy surface with scattered rocks and a distant outcrop. No burned-in captions or mission clocks are visible on screen; spoken narration mentions the Perseverance rover and its cameras, geochemistry instruments, and a subsurface radar.
evidence.title: Perseverance Explores Ancient River Channel (Mars Report)

evidence.query: Rover close-ups of rounded pebbles, cross-bedded sedimentary layers and conglomerate rocks with wheel tracks nearby.
evidence.text: Wide-angle, color images of a reddish, rocky slope on Mars showing layered bedrock and patches of wind-blown, rippled sand. Multiple, parallel rover wheel tracks with a distinct tread pattern cross the sandy patches; part of the rover deck/wheel area is visible at the lower left. A text annotation (MARKER BAND, CURIOSITY ROVER TRACKS) with arrows points to a linear band of repetitively spaced, flat rock slabs on the slope. An inset close-up box shows the same flat, thin-bedded rock fragments with regular spacing and surface lamination/striations, highlighting the repetitive pattern referenced in the narration.
evidence.title: NASA’s Curiosity Rover Finds New Clues to Mars’ Watery Past
